title: Epistolae Sex Ad Diversos
author: Columbanus Hibernus
source: Translated by Claude from tmp1347.tmp1347.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.

passages.original: Quid ergo dicis de Pascha XXI aut XXII lunae, quod jam (tua [Ms., tui] tamen pace dictum sit) non esse Pas- cha, nimirum tenebrosum a multis comprobatur e calcalenteris? Non latet enim, ut credo, efficaciam tuam, quantum Anatolius, mirae doctrinae vir, ut sanctus ait Hieronymus, cujus Eusebius Caesariensis episcopus in ecclesiastica Excerpta inseruit Historia (sic), et sanctus Hieronymus in suo hoc idem de Pascha opus collaudavit Catalogo, de hac lunae aetate vitu- perando disputet; qui contra Gallicanos Rimarios de Pascha, ut ait, errantes, horrendam intulit sen- tentiam : Certe, inquietis, si usque ad duarum vigi- liarum terminum quod noctis medium indicat, ortus lunae tardaverit, non lux tenebras, sed lucem tenebrae superant;
passages.english: What then do you say about an Easter on the twenty-first or twenty-second [day] of the moon, which (be it said, however, with your leave) is not Easter, being indeed a dark [one], as is proved by many calculators? For it does not escape your excellency, I believe, how strongly Anatolius, a man of wonderful learning, as Saint Jerome says, whose excerpts Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, inserted into [his] Ecclesiastical History, and whose same work on Easter Saint Jerome praised in his Catalogue, argues in censure of this age of the moon; he, against the Gallican reckoners who, as he says, err about Easter, delivered a dreadful judgement: "Certainly," you will say, "if the rising of the moon is delayed up to the limit of the two watches, which marks the middle of the night, it is not light that overcomes darkness, but darkness that overcomes light;"
passages.notes: "e calcalenteris" is evidently corrupt; I have taken it as a garbled form of "calculatoribus" (calculators, computists), which is uncertain. "Rimarios" is obscure; I have read it as a corruption of a word for computists/reckoners (perhaps "numerarios" or "calculatores"); the sense is uncertain. "tua [Ms., tui]": the edition notes the manuscript reads "tui"; the sense is unaffected. "(sic)" is the editor's mark and has been omitted from the translation. The quoted words are attributed to Anatolius, who addresses his opponents in the second person plural ("you will say").
